IV. Correctly Explaining the Scriptural Text (2). There are two parts to the correct explanation of the scriptural text:
first, explaining the title; second, interpreting the main body of the text.
First, explaining the title.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-urundabhaṇa-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Ullambana Bowl) has three translations in total:
first, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, the Dharma Master Fashu translated it as the *Ullambana Sūtra*.

2. During the reign of Emperor Hui, Dharma Master Faju translated [this text] as the *Guanla jing* (Sutra on the Offering of Incense and Cakes). This title corresponds to the passage in the present text which states: "Providing food of a hundred flavors, the five fruits, water-jars for sprinkling, fragrant oil, lamps, candles, and so forth."

Third, regarding the Old Edition’s Separate Record (*bielu*), there was also a master who translated it as the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), establishing its title based on the practices performed therein.
What is being explained here is precisely the first translation.
The Tripitaka Master Yijing said:
"That which is proclaimed from my own mouth and communicated to the minds of others is called 'the Buddha's teaching' because the instruction accords with the capacity of the recipient.
*Ullambana* is a term from the Western Regions; in this [Chinese] language, it means "hanging upside down."
The *pen* (basin) is a term from the Eastern Xia; it is traditionally used as a vessel for salvation.
If one were to follow local customs, it should be called the "Basin for Saving Those Hanging Upside Down.

This is because the Venerable One’s own soul had sunk into the dark path, suffering both hunger and thirst with a life as precarious as being suspended upside down; even with the majestic spiritual power of the Holy Son [the Buddha], there would have been no way to rescue him from such misery and ruin.

The Buddha commanded that a hundred flavors be offered in a basin as a formal tribute to the Triple Gem; by looking up to the grace and radiance of the Great Assembly, one is rescued from the urgency of being suspended upside down. It is from this meaning that the title of the sutra is established.
"Sūtra" (jing) is properly named "thread" (sūtra), and its meaning is called "Sūtra of Accordance" (Kie-king).

A thread can string together flowers, and a warp-thread can hold the woof; this means that the meanings explained are like the flowers or the woof, while the words that explain them can hold and string them together.
Now, following the terminology of these local scriptures and edicts, it is designated as a "Sūtra" (Jing).
To clarify its meaning and assist in its naming, the character "Qie" (契) has been added.

This interpretation accords with the sense of "pervasion" among the two meanings given in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, and with the sense of "garland" among the five meanings given in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
2. Explanation of the Main Text.
The explanation of the main text is divided into three parts:
first, the introductory section (nidāna); second, the main body (śarīra); and third, the dissemination section (pariṇāmanā).
With its threefold arising, it spans the heavens with its lofty judgment; it darkly accords with the Western Regions and is followed alike by the present and the past.
Within the initial *nidāna* section, many sūtras contain two types of prefaces:
first, the *śraddhā-prasāda-nidāna* (preface of testimony and faith), which states: "Thus have I heard this Dharma from the Buddha."
The time and place of the teaching are clearly marked so that the great assembly may hear them together without error; this serves as evidence to ensure universal faith and acceptance.
Whether the sūtra is extensive or concise, it is not transmitted without faith; therefore, at the beginning of every sūtra, there must be a statement of testimony and faith (*saddharmapratyaya*).
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The time, place, and persons are mentioned in order to inspire faith.
Second is the introductory section on the occasion (*nidāna-parivarta*), which inspires faith and gives rise to the Dharma of the main teaching.
This is as seen in examples such as the "Jewel Canopy" in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the "Light from the Ūrṇā-hair" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the "Certification of Faith" (the introductory formula) is also called the "General Preface," because it is common to all sūtras.
It is also called the "Postscript to the Sūtra," because it did not exist at the time the Buddha preached the Dharma.
It is also called the "Introductory Section" (*nidāna*), because each sūtra has its own distinct introduction.
It is also called the "Preface to the Sūtra," because the Buddha first initiates the discourse himself before expounding the main body of the teaching.
First, the Prologue of Certification and Faith.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Thus, when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda requested instruction on four matters, which the Buddha directed him to set aside for later.

Regarding these four matters that were asked, the Buddha answered each one individually: first, to rely upon the four foundations of mindfulness; second, to take the precepts as one's teacher; third, to silence and exclude monks of ill-natured character; and fourth, to state at the beginning of all sūtras: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in such-and-such a place together with such-and-such a number of people."

Most sūtras possess six kinds of accomplishments; though the phrasing may be abbreviated, the meaning must necessarily include them. These are: first, faith; second, hearing; third, time; fourth, the teacher; fifth, the location; and sixth, the assembly.
If the six conditions are not fulfilled, the teaching will not flourish.
It is necessary for all six to be present; therefore, it is said that they are "accomplished.
In the present sutra, however, the assembly is omitted.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) appears at the beginning and differs from other sutras, these are each the stylistic choices of the respective translators.

That is to say, some state, "Such a Dharma as this I have heard from the Buddha," while others state, "I have heard such a Dharma from the side of the Buddha"; both are expressions used to point to the Dharma.
The reason it does not say "I" is that it intends to demonstrate that all sages have realized the principle of non-self (*anātman*).

As for its occurrence in other sutras, it refers to Ānanda himself pointing to the conventional designations of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); this is not the "self" imagined by ordinary people, and thus there is no fault.
"Having heard" means that the ear-faculty gives rise to consciousness to listen to those external sounds.
The subsequent phrase "in this way" refers to the accomplishment of faith.
For one who has faith says, "This matter is thus," while one who lacks faith says, "This matter is not thus."
Therefore, Master Sengzhao said:
"It is a term signifying faith and compliance.
As for "one time," it refers to the complete process of teaching and listening when teacher and disciple are assembled together; taken as a whole, it is called "one time."
This serves to distinguish it from other times.

That is to say, when the Tathāgata preached the sūtras, there were immeasurable occasions; since they cannot be cited individually, the term "once" is used as a concise summary that encompasses them all.
Since the duration of time varies across different regions and is not fixed, it is generally stated as "at one time.
However, when various sūtras do not specify the time or the location, some interpretations have given rise to difficulties; therefore, such a practice is not adopted here.

Now, examining his intent in detail: as for their locations, they do not exceed the sixteen kingdoms where he wandered, transformed beings, and resided; thus, they can be easily identified and pointed out.

At that time, the periods of years, months, spring, autumn, winter, and summer; cold and heat; day and night; and moments such as the *yīn* and *mǎo* hours—all these temporal variations change with such rapidity, their accumulation being so immeasurable that they cannot be recorded or described, and are difficult to point out or define.
"Buddha" is the Sanskrit term *buddha*, which here means "the Awakened One. This refers to one who has fully realized the nature and characteristics of both the true and the delusive.
There are three meanings of "awakening":
first, self-awakening to the emptiness of the self, which distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary beings.
Second, awakening to the emptiness of the dharmas of others distinguishes [this stage] from that of the Two Vehicles.

Third, awakening to the full emptiness of both [self and others] accords with original enlightenment; it is termed ultimate awakening or great, wondrous awakening, distinguishing it from that of the Bodhisattvas.
Regarding "at Śrāvastī and so forth," this refers to the perfection of the location.
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* commentary states: "There are two kinds of dwelling places:
first, the sphere of activity, which refers to those who transform while remaining among the laity."
The two places of reliance refer to those who govern the community of renunciants:
the former is Śrāvastī, and the latter is Jetavana.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "By mentioning Śrāvastī, people from afar are made aware [of the teaching]."
To cite Jetavana is to make it known to those nearby.

Śrāvastī is translated here as "Hearing of Things" (Wénwù), meaning that because it abounds in wealth and treasures, and because people who possess great learning and liberation are heard of from afar throughout all lands.
The Tripitaka Master Yijing’s translation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* refers to it as the "Great City of Renown.
Regarding the Jeta Grove and so forth, these refer to the trees donated by Prince Jeta and the park purchased by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Jeta, which in this language means "Victorious in Battle," was the crown prince of King Prasenajit.
He was given this name because at the time of his birth, the king had achieved victory over foreign nations in battle.
Anāthapiṇḍada was the title of this minister; his original name was Sudatta, which means "Good Giver. Thus, Anāthapiṇḍada is synonymous with Good Giver.

Furthermore, because he constantly practiced giving, he was called "Virtuous Giver" (Śūradatta), and his fellow villagers praised him with the title "Giver to the Lonely and Destitute" (Anāthapiṇḍada).

Now, while the garden was purchased by Sudatta and the trees were donated by Jeta, the garden represents the whole and the trees represent the parts; thus, one would normally designate the garden first. However, in this case, to distinguish between the noble and the humble according to propriety, the trees are mentioned before the garden.
In the Western lands, a monastery is called *saṃghārāma*, which in this [Middle Kingdom] means "garden of the community.
When Buddhism first flowed eastward and reached China, foreign monks were accommodated in the Court of State Ceremonial (*hónglù sì*).
As the number of monks gradually increased, they were dispersed into separate residences; these retained their original designation and are all called "monasteries" (*sì*).
Regarding those who purchased gardens and donated trees, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
When the elder Sudatta went to Rājagṛha to arrange a marriage for his son, he encountered the Buddha there.
Having awakened the aspiration for enlightenment, he invited the Buddha to Śrāvastī to preach the Dharma.
The Buddha instructed Śāriputra to follow him back and first select a place to stay.
He chose Prince Jeta’s grove; when the elder asked to purchase it, the prince said jokingly, "If you can cover it entirely by spreading gold coins side by side, then I shall sell it."
The elder then wished to hand it over,
but the prince said,
"That was a joke."
They invited an arbitrator to settle the matter, and he adjudicated it according to the former statement.
The elder spread out his gold on the ground, leaving only one corner uncovered.

Seeing that he did not begrudge his wealth and treasures, the prince realized the Buddha’s extraordinary excellence; he then offered the remaining ground to establish a gateway and donated the trees in the garden to provide shade for a grove.
The two of them together completed the vihāra and invited the Buddha to reside there; thus it is said, "the Jeta Grove," and so forth.
As for the omission of the "accomplishment by the assembly," it is merely a textual abbreviation, as seen in the *Anityatā-sūtra* and other such works.

However, there is a specific time when one must necessarily possess a retinue of followers; therefore, the end of the sutra states: "The fourfold assembly of disciples rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
This concludes the sixth section: the Prologue of the Occasion.

Regarding the "Initiation": since this sutra takes filial piety and the extraction from suffering as its central theme, it employs the occasion of rescuing one's mother as the catalyst for its inception.
The text is divided into six sections: first, Maudgalyāyana’s attainment of the Way;

second, his awareness of gratitude and desire to repay it; third, his yearning and exhaustive search; fourth, his discovery of her location; fifth, his weeping and departure to rescue her; and sixth, the manifestation of his past evil habits.
First, Maudgalyāyana’s path was perfected.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana first attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
This person’s clan name was Mahāmaudgalyāyana; in the language of Tang, it means "of the Mung-bean lineage."
In ancient times, there was a seer in that country who always ate mung beans; the Venerable One is of his lineage.
His name is Nyagrodha, which is also the name of a tree.
The Venerable One’s two parents offered a sacrifice to this tree deity and thereby gave birth to him; thus it was named after this.
He was the son of a high minister in the city of Rājagṛha; because people of the time esteemed his lineage, he was addressed by his clan name.

Regarding "one who has first attained the six supernormal powers": "first" means the beginning; it refers to one who, upon first attaining the Noble Path, immediately delivers their two parents, because they originally cultivated the Way on account of their parents.
Although the Path itself is without difference, original vows vary; therefore, it is not necessarily the case that all sages act in this manner.
Regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*): first is the power of the miraculous domain (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), so called because one realizes the miraculous domain through wisdom.
It is also termed the power of mastery over the will (*kāma-avaśitva*), for the body reaches wherever one intends to go, just as the will desires.

Second is the supernormal power of the divine eye; third is the supernormal power of the divine ear; these refer to the ability to see and hear forms, sounds, and so forth, whether near or far, and whether obstructed or unobstructed.
Fourth is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, which enables one to know the original births and fundamental events of previous existences.

Fifth is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*), which means being able to know all states of mind, whether concentrated or distracted, and whether tainted or untainted.
Sixth is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), which means being able to know that the outflows within one’s own body have been exhausted.
The six [senses] are all without obstruction; therefore, they are collectively termed "penetrating.
Second, there is the desire to repay kindness:
one wishes to deliver one's parents to repay the kindness of their nursing.
"Deliverance" (du) means to deliver and liberate.
However, the two characters "repaying kindness" (bao'en) serve merely as a general placeholder; "delivering and liberating" is precisely what constitutes that repayment.
"Milk" refers to maternal milk, and "feeding" (bu) refers to chewing and feeding.
However, there are degrees of distance between parents, degrees of lightness or gravity in their kindness, and degrees of partiality or completeness in the repayment of that kindness.
"Distant" refers to seven generations or even more; "proximate" refers to those who have given birth to this very body.
The "seven generations" is a doctrine followed by non-Buddhist teachings.

People take physical form as their fundamental essence; as they transmit this substance through continuous succession, they regard the seven generations beginning with one's father and grandfather as paramount, and thus show particular veneration for the father.

The fundamental tenet of Buddhism is that human beings take the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their essence, while the four great elements and physical form serve as the basis upon which this spiritual consciousness relies. In every successive life, one has parents; from those who gave birth to and nurtured this current body, extending back through seven lifetimes, the parents of each birth constitute the "seven generations."

However, the place where one is entrusted is solely the mother's womb; furthermore, from birth, it is mostly the mother who provides nourishment through breastfeeding and embraces one in her arms. Thus, the mother is emphasized above all others, and for this reason, the sutras speak only of repaying the kindness of her nursing.

Regarding "even through many lifetimes," this specifically refers to taking refuge in one's biological parents from the time of that refuge onward, because they were able to give birth to one's body, which serves as the vessel for practicing the Path.
When the Buddhas attain enlightenment, their parents of many lifetimes all meet one another and hear the Dharma, thereby gaining benefit.
Regarding the gravity of this kindness, the parents of this present life are the most significant, while those of other lives are progressively lighter.

Regarding "repaying a portion" versus "repaying the whole": serving and supporting one throughout a single lifetime constitutes a portion; liberating them through many lifetimes constitutes the whole.
Thus, a sutra says: "Carrying one's father on the left shoulder and one's mother on the right shoulder, and traveling across the entire earth, one still could not repay their kindness."
Thus we know that what is retributed in this life constitutes one's lot (*bhāga*); even if one were equal to Mengzong, Dong’an, or Dong Yong, these too would constitute one's lot.
Now the Sūtra says: "Those who wish to deliver their parents intend to cause them to attain the Way."
This clarifies that [filial piety] is complete.
If one fails to repay [this debt] altogether, one is already an unfilial sinner; how much more so when one commits acts of rebellion against it?
Furthermore, to speak generally of the kindness owed by all people, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Those who do not recognize kindness will frequently meet with untimely deaths."
The *Buddhānusmṛtya-samudra-lakṣaṇa-sūtra* states: "To fail to repay kindness is a cause for rebirth in the Avīci Hell.
This applies even to ordinary debts of gratitude, let alone those owed to one's parents.
The kindness of one's parents is beyond measure; thus, the *Shijing* says: "Tall and luxuriant are the young elms, yet they are not elms but weeds.
Alas for my parents! How weary was their toil in bringing me into this world."
There was no father to rely upon and no mother to depend on; when he went out, he carried his grief with him, and when he returned, there was no one to welcome him home.
"Father gave me life; Mother nurtured me. She stroked me and raised me, she grew me and nourished me."
"I look at you and again at you; you enter and exit my very belly.
I wish to repay your virtue, yet it is as vast as Heaven and has no limit.
Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master said:

"The righteousness of one's parents is as lofty as heaven and earth, and their kindness is as deep as the vast ocean; therefore, one looks up with longing, mindful of the grace of nourishing them in the womb, and reflects upon how to repay their labor and virtue.

The *Sutra on the Profound Kindness of Parents* states: "When parents embrace their child, they smile without speaking, harmoniously making cooing sounds. When hungry, the child must have food, and none but the mother provides it; when thirsty, the child must have drink, and none but the mother offers her milk," and so forth.
When I calculate and deliberate upon my mother’s kindness, it is as vast as the great heavens and beyond measure.
Alas! How can I ever repay my compassionate mother?
Thus it was that when traveling to and fro between the eastern and western neighborhoods, or visiting wells, hearths, mortars, and water-mills, I would not return home at regular intervals.
The mother was suddenly startled, and milk flowed from both her breasts; she immediately knew that her son at home was missing her, and she returned home at once.
Question:
Question: Examining this scriptural passage, why does it specifically admonish those of poor and lowly status?
Answer:
The gentleman practices filial piety naturally; therefore, the scripture specifically admonishes the common people.
Furthermore, even if a gentleman suffers the poverty of a single bamboo basket and a gourd ladle, what impediment does this pose to such matters as grinding grain?
Moreover, the specific accounts of hardship and toil merely serve to manifest the labor involved in his upbringing.

It further says: "When the child saw his mother coming from afar, he would sometimes shake his head and wag his rump while standing in a carriage, or again, he would drag his belly along as he walked, crying out toward his mother."
The mother bends her body down toward her child, stretching out both hands to rub away the dust and dirt; she kisses his mouth, opens her heart to yield her milk, and nourishes him with that milk.
The mother sees her child with joy, and the child sees his mother with delight; their mutual affection and compassionate love are so profound that nothing can surpass them, and so forth.

Once he has grown up, he is accompanied by friends as they comb his hair and groom his locks. Desiring fine garments to clothe his body, the parents wear their own old and tattered clothes, while the new and fine silks are first given to their son.
As for those traveling on urgent official or private business, who tilt their hearts toward the south or north and pursue their sons to the east or west, they wear it crosswise upon their heads.

As the son gradually grows up, she seeks a wife for him; having obtained another girl, her parents become increasingly estranged, while she and her lover converse and take pleasure together in the privacy of her chamber.
When one’s parents have grown old and their strength has declined, yet they do not come to inquire after them from morning until evening;
or if the father is widowed and the mother is a widow, dwelling alone in an empty room like a traveler staying in another’s house, they will constantly lack affection and love.
Some, lacking tunics, suffer the bitterness of cold and frost; they encounter such extreme calamities that their hardships are too great.
As they grow old and their appearance fades, they become rife with fleas and lice; unable to sleep day or night, they sigh and lament:
"By what sin or karmic transgression from a past life have I given birth to such unfilial children?"
At times he would call out to them, but they met his glaring eyes with anger and defiance, refusing to obey him at all.
When his wife and children reviled him, he would lower his head and smile, saying nothing.

Śakra, Brahmā, the various devas, and the people—all those in the assembly—rejoiced upon hearing the sutra and resolved their minds on Bodhicitta; they wept aloud until the earth shook and their tears fell like rain.
The commentary states:
"Reflecting carefully upon this matter, these words are indeed true.
There may be mothers who are not like this or sons who are not like that, but such cases do not occur even once in a hundred."

This is truly because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded by ignorance, clinging to the false while alienated from the truth; since their fundamental root is inverted, every branch and detail is likewise so.
Alas for the ignorant and foolish! How can they be delivered?
Third, seeking through longing:
one observes the world with the eye of the Path (mārgacakṣus).
Observing the places where beings are born is the supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣur-abhijñā).
Because it is attained through the realization of the Path, it is called the "Path-eye.
There are two types of worlds: namely, the container world, which refers to the three realms, and the sentient-being world, which refers to the six destinies.
However, on the day the Venerable One lost his parents, he was still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and did not know in which realm his parents had been reborn.

Now that he has attained the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*), his power enables him to seek this out; thus, with his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he surveys upward and downward, searching for their bodies within the six realms of existence throughout the three worlds.
Having attained the contemplation of penetration, he spoke of "immediacy.
Fourth, he attained the vision of her location:
he saw his deceased mother born among the hungry ghosts, unable to see food or drink, with skin and bone standing together.

When originally observing the world, one seeks out both parents; however, the father who gives birth to one in a realm of happiness does not require such arduous effort, and since this is not the primary tenet of the Sūtra, it is not described here.

As for the mother who gives birth to one in the realm of hungry ghosts, she already belongs to the three miserable paths (*tridurgati*), and furthermore, being among the starving, she experiences the ultimate suffering of a ghost. To rescue those in such suffering, there is only the *Ullambana* bowl; the intent behind establishing the True Teaching lies precisely in this.
Being born among the hungry ghosts is the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), as it compensates for the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).
Not seeing food and drink is the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), as it compensates for the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*); this is the fruit of the karma of stinginess and greed.
Standing there with skin and bone joined is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, the original abode of the hungry ghosts (*preta*) is five hundred yojanas beneath this continent, and its length and breadth are likewise the same.

There is the realm of Yama; proceeding from here and dispersing toward other directions, one month in the human world constitutes one day there, and by accumulating such months and years, their lifespan reaches five hundred years.
However, there are three kinds of ghosts:
first, the "ghosts without wealth" (*niḥsvabhoga*), who, because they lack merit, are unable to obtain food;
second, the "ghosts with little wealth" (*alpasvabhoga*), who obtain only a small amount of pure and exquisite food and drink.
Third, the ghosts with abundant wealth, so called because they obtain pure and exquisite food and drink in great quantities.
These three types of ghosts each further have three subdivisions.
Regarding the three types of those without wealth: first, the torch-mouthed ghosts (*ulkāmukha*), meaning that blazing torches constantly issue from their mouths.

Consequently, because in a previous life he burned down village fences and roasted the virtuous and worthy in order to seek wealth, he fell into hell; having emerged from hell, he has now fallen among these ghosts.

Thus, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "If a person, out of greed and envy, unjustly seizes the wealth of others, destroys their cities and fortresses, or kills, plunders, and acquires riches to present to kings and high ministers, thereby increasing their own cruelty and violence, they will fall into the realm of the blazing hungry ghosts."
2. The Needle-Necked Ghosts: These have heads as large as mountains and throats like the eye of a needle.
This is due to their breaking the precepts by eating at night and stealing the food of the Sangha.

Therefore, the *Cai fa qingjing jing* (Sūtra on the Purity of the Method of Fasting) states: "Maudgalyāyana encountered several million ghosts on the road, their heads as large as great mountains," and so forth.
Third are the stinking-mouth ghosts (*pūti-mukha-piśāca*), who suffer because the putrid stench from their mouths is loathsome to themselves.
Because of excessive craving for fame and profit, asserting one's own rightness while disparaging others, praising the wicked and slandering the virtuous—
for these three reasons, it would be better to swallow iron balls than to consume the offerings of the faithful.
The three types of beings with sparse wealth are: first, the *sūcīmukha* (needle-haired) ghosts, whose hair is as sharp as needles; when they walk, it pierces them of its own accord.
Because of their greed for profit, they falsely practice acupuncture and moxibustion, or pierce livestock, seeking only wealth rather than curing illnesses.
Second, the stinking-haired spirits (*pūtimukha-piśāca*): their hair is coarse and foul-smelling, and they suffer by plucking it out themselves.

This results from the trade in pigs and sheep, and the slaughter of geese and ducks; as their bodies are scalded in boiling water and flayed with knives, the agony is unbearable. When their retribution in hell ends, they fall into this realm of hungry ghosts.
Third, the *mahāgalagaṇḍa* spirits: with large goiters hanging from their throats, they pierce them themselves to consume the pus.
This is because they were constantly harboring resentment and anger due to jealousy toward others.
Regarding the three types of those with abundant wealth: first, the *ucchistabhojana* spirits, so called because they constantly obtain food discarded during sacrifices.
First, because their sins are many and their merits few, they give only after having discarded what was intended for others due to their extreme stinginess.
Second, the "gain-and-loss" ghosts (prāptāprāpta-preta), who constantly obtain food discarded in the streets and alleys.
This is because they constantly give rise to stinginess and attachment toward present wealth, and only relinquish it when they suspect of losing it.
Third, the spirits of power, namely yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and so forth.

The wealth and pleasures they enjoy are similar to those of humans and devas; whether dwelling in forests, residing in mountain valleys, living in spirit shrines, or staying in empty palaces, they move upright on their feet and belong to the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati).

These various and manifold transformations arise because, during the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), one's offenses and merits were not pure, and the causes of suffering and happiness were produced in a state of mutual intermingling.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃgraha* (or *Dharmatrāta-dharmaguptaka-śāstra*) states:
The bhikṣu Saṃghayaśas was traveling along the shore of the great ocean when he saw a magnificent palace; within it, his own family members were locking up two ghosts and others.
The relatives of the Venerable One are now *kuntapāpika* pretas among the wealthless pretas.
Furthermore, it is stated in another source that there are three kinds of pretas:
first, those with external obstructions (*bāhyāvaraṇa*), who, upon encountering water, see people wielding swords, staves, and other weapons obstructing them.
2. Internal obstacles (*antarāya*): having a torch in one's mouth, or a throat as narrow as a needle.
3. Obstacles of non-existence (*anantarāya*): seeing the river as a fierce fire, or eating excrement and filth, or cutting off and eating one's own flesh, and so forth.
"Now, the Venerable One's own kinsmen shall act as internal obstacles.

All the various ghosts encountered thus far have been summoned by the causes and actions of their own minds; the retribution must inevitably correspond to its cause, just as shadows and echoes arise from forms and sounds. Even one's parents and closest kin cannot substitute for one another."

Therefore, all wise ones should each exert their minds; if you should encounter favorable conditions, you must not let them pass in vain. Once one has departed this life, who will perform the rites of veneration?
Even if one entrusts the matter to one's descendants, they will likely reap but one-seventh of the merit;
how much more so if there is no filial son—then what can be done to remedy such regret?

Furthermore, in this turbid world, the common masses rarely cherish benevolence and filial piety; they worry only for their wives and children—how could they ever think of the spirits in the netherworld?

The poor and lowly are oppressed by hunger and cold, while the wealthy and noble are dissipated by riches and sensual pleasures. Even if they were to pursue merit, those who weary of their duties are many;
those who exert their full strength and empty their hearts are one in ten thousand.
The ways of the world are witnessed by our very eyes; how could they not be manifest?

Thus, the *Enzhong jing* (Sutra on the Profundity of Gratitude) says: "If husband and wife together commit the five heinous crimes, at that time [the victim] will call out as they hurriedly run and drive him away."
"When their parents speak, they disobey nine times out of ten; they do not follow or obey them, but instead revile them and glare with angry eyes.
If they are thus even while alive, what can be expected after death?
Since they themselves are not benevolent, how could their children possibly be filial?"
Therefore, in the past, there was one who followed his father into the forest and wilderness, and then took up the carriage to return home.
Observing the present through the lens of antiquity, although the paths and traces differ, the intent of the heart is the same.
Fifth, wailing in grief as he went to rescue him.
Maudgalyāyana was filled with sorrow and immediately took rice in his alms bowl to go and feed his mother.
As for this sorrow: the debt of gratitude for the kindness of giving birth and raising one is as heavy as previously described.

To suddenly meet again after the separation of death and the interval of rebirth—even if one’s appearance remained unchanged—would cause tears and grief; how much more so when seeing a ghostly form where skin and bone stand together, with smoke and flames in the throat and an empty belly? Suffering like one whose life-vein is overturned and who survives only by gasping for breath, how could he not break his body with wild leaps and exhaust his breath in wailing, lamenting the self-indulgence of his sinful rebellion and grieving that his compassionate parent was undergoing such suffering?

The Sūtra sets forth its general purport by simply stating "sorrowful lamentation" (*beiai*); yet, if one examines the circumstances of that time closely, what doubt could there be that it was not so?
Therefore, the Tripitaka Master’s topical outline (*ke*) uses the term "crushing wailing" (*cuītòng*), and his commentary explains:
"The emotion stirs to the very marrow of the bones; the cries shake heaven and earth."

Regarding "taking a bowl of rice to visit and provide sustenance": since the mother’s breath was already faint and she was suffering from the calamity of exhaustion at evening, she was now facing the distress of morning hunger; being both hungry and thirsty, she stood in need of relief, and for such an emergency, food and drink were the priority. Therefore, he took rice in his alms-bowl and carried it to provide for his mother.
Sixth, the manifestation of past evil habits:
When her mother received a bowl of rice, she shielded the bowl with her left hand and tried to grasp the food with her right.
Before the food had even entered her mouth, it transformed into glowing coals, so that she was unable to eat.
Objects transform according to the mind, and results are accomplished through karma.
If the cause of hunger has not been eliminated, how can the condition for satiety be brought about?
The hungry ghosts have flaming mouths; when food approaches their mouths, it bursts into flames.
Water turns into hard ice; it is only when ice approaches boiling water that it becomes solid.

Thus one knows that supernatural power cannot restrain the force of karma. To eliminate hunger, one must first eliminate stinginess; therefore, although the six supernormal powers allowed him to go and provide food, he brought calamity upon himself, and though a basin was laid out with a hundred flavors, it resulted in suffering.
How great is the ripening of karma—how truly worthy of reflection!
Now, with his left hand he shields the bowl, fearing that others might encroach upon it;
with his right hand he pats the food, craving only for his own sustenance.
Since their stinginess and greed are so fierce that they manifest in this way, how could they be sustained by inferior food?
Therefore, he transformed it into fire so that they could not eat.
This concludes the introductory section.
II. The Main Body of the Text (Zhengzongfen). This section is divided into two parts:
first, Maudgalyāyana’s sorrowful recounting of his suffering and distress; second, the Tathāgata’s extensive exposition of the causes and conditions.
First, Maudgalyāyana lamented his bitter distress.
Maudgalyāyana cried out in grief and wept profusely; he hurried back to inform the Buddha, recounting the matter in detail.
A son must urgently inform his father, and a minister must urgently inform his sovereign; when one’s own strength is insufficient, it is only right to seek refuge with the Buddha.
Your disciple has diligently contemplated the Four Noble Truths and already realized the Three Insights; he could turn mountains and rivers upside down or cause the sun and moon to revolve.

Yet, I did not expect that my mother would be entangled in such extreme suffering, her life hanging by a thread. Though I exhausted my filial sincerity and displayed all my spiritual transformations, I was ultimately unable to eliminate her karmic retribution or temporarily relieve her starving belly. Therefore, I have returned running with wailing cries, fully expressing my grief and earnest pleas.
II. The Tathāgata’s Extensive Demonstration of Causes and Conditions (Hetu-pratyaya) in Eight Parts.
The Tathāgata’s extensive demonstration of causes and conditions is broadly divided into eight sections according to the Tripiṭaka:

first, revealing the profound gravity of the mother’s transgression; second, clarifying the inferiority of the son’s virtues; third, censuring the powerlessness of heterodoxy; fourth, manifesting the efficacy of the orthodox path; fifth, granting the means of salvation; sixth, demonstrating the true Dharma; seventh, the filial son’s realization; and eighth, the compassionate mother’s attainment of benefit.
First, to reveal the depth of the mother’s transgression,
the Buddha said:
“The roots of your mother’s transgressions are deep and firmly entangled.”
In a certain sutra it is said:
During the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Maudgalyāyana was named Rābu and his mother’s name was Qingti.
As Rābu was about to depart, he entrusted his mother with these words:
"If any guests should come, you must prepare a meal for them.
After she had left, when the guest arrived, the mother failed to provide any food; instead, she continued her deception by pretending to have laid out a banquet.
The son returned and asked,
"When the guests arrived yesterday, how did you prepare for them?
His mother replied:
“Did you not see the place where the food was being prepared?
From that time onward, throughout five hundred lifetimes, his stinginess has continued in succession; therefore, it is said that the roots of his transgressions are deeply entangled.
"Sin" refers to the karma of body and speech; "root" refers to the mind of stinginess and greed.
When these arise repeatedly in succession, they become deep; when they are firmly entwined and difficult to untie, they become "knots.
All that arises from stinginess constitutes sinful karma, not merely the single instance of false speech at that time.
This means that stinginess is the root of suffering, its actions are the karma of suffering, and hungry ghosts are the fruit of suffering; these constitute the three matters.
If one follows the ten grave precepts, stinginess is also considered karma, while greed alone is the root, because it gives rise to sinful karma.
Question:
For five hundred lifetimes, one was stingy; was this as a human or as a ghost?
Answer:
Humans and ghosts exist in alternation, and their creation and reception of karma mutually support one another.
If there were only human bodies, they could not be called retributions for evil; if there were only ghostly bodies, they would have no basis for creating karma.
It is also not logically precluded that they may become animals.
However, as long as the habit of stinginess has not been eliminated, it is termed "continuity.
Question:
Since the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Maudgalyāyana has had many different mothers throughout his successive births; why does he single out and rescue only his mother Candikā?
Answer:
Ceti’s karmic connection with Maudgalyāyana was profound; in this life, she has once again become his mother.
He merely saved the mother who gave birth to his current body; it does not mean he saved that distant past Ceti.
The various other arguments and so forth are all based on a failure to reach [the truth].
Second, explaining the inferiority of the son's merit:
"It is not something that can be remedied by the power of you alone."
"Your mother was stingy, being miserly toward everything.
Time has passed through many lifetimes and you have encountered many people; how could you alone have the power to rescue her?"
3. Reprimanding the Deceitful and Powerlessness:

"Though your filial piety moves heaven and earth, neither the celestial deities and terrestrial spirits, nor the demons, heretics, Daoist masters, or the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings can do anything about it."
The Tripitaka Master said:

"Even if you were to move celestial spirits in the upper realms and stir earth deities in the lower regions; even if you were to subdue malevolent demons and ensnare heretics from all sides; even if you were to unify the six directions into a single family and consolidate the eight classes of beings into one assembly—none of these would avail you, for even with such supernatural powers, nothing could be done."
"Non-Buddhist practitioners (waidao daoshi)" refers to those who are practitioners among the non-Buddhists, distinguishing them from practitioners within the Buddhist path.
This is because when Buddhism was first transmitted to this region, monks were addressed as "practitioners" (daoshi).
The Four Heavenly Kings are Vaiśravaṇa and others who protect and sustain the world.
Fourth, it reveals that there is the capacity [to act] correctly:
"One must rely on the majestic spiritual power of the Sangha of the ten directions in order to attain liberation."
The Tripiṭaka Master said:
"A single thread cannot restrain an elephant; one must rely on many strands.
A single person cannot eliminate karma; one must depend upon a multitude of virtues."
Now, examining the preceding and following scriptural passages, there are four propositions based on the contrast between the false and the correct, and the one and the many:
first, that which is correct but not manifold; this cannot provide salvation, as indicated previously by the words, "How can you alone save [others]?"
Second, those who are numerous but not correct cannot provide salvation; this refers to the aforementioned "gods, spirits, malevolent demons, and non-Buddhists," and so forth.
Third, only those who are both numerous and correct can provide rescue and extraction; this refers to the Sangha of the ten directions.
4. As for "not much" and "not correct," these are inherently untenable; therefore, there is no scriptural passage [addressing them].
5. Granting this as a means of rescue:
"I shall now expound the method of salvation, so that all who face difficulties may be freed from sorrow and suffering."
The phrase "I shall now explain" is precisely a term of assent.
"The Dharma of rescue and relief" refers to the matter being assented to.

Regarding the phrase "causing all to be equal": a crossbow of a thousand *jin* does not discharge its trigger solely for a field mouse; how could the Honored One of the Three Realms unilaterally cause only your mother to be freed from suffering?
Sixth, showing them the True Dharma.
Showing the True Dharma is divided into two parts:
first, teaching the method for the filial son to present offerings; second, teaching the ritual for the assembly of monks to receive the offerings.
Initially, there are five further points:

first, determining the superior time; second, generating the superior intention; third, providing the superior offering; fourth, praising the superior field; and fifth, attaining the superior benefit.
This means that the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is the most excellent time, like the month of spring’s warmth;
filial piety is the most excellent intention, like a fresh and high-quality seed;
and the hundred flavors and five fruits are the most excellent offerings, like a fine ox and a plow.
To make offerings with these is like being able to cultivate and till the soil; the sages and saints serve as the supreme field of merit, like fertile ground rich in fatness.

To ensure that deceased parents, six degrees of kin, and even ancestors up to the seventh generation leave suffering behind and are reborn in heaven constitutes a supreme benefit, like harvesting thousands of chests and tens of thousands of bushels in autumn and storing them for winter.
Is not the purport of the sūtra’s textual flow evident in this way?
Let the wise examine it closely; it will be as clear as pointing at one's own palm.
First: The Fivefold Method for Filial Sons to Present Offerings.
First, the excellence of the time.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the monks of the ten directions observe the *pravāraṇā* ceremony."
The Sanskrit term *saṃgha* is translated here as "the harmony of the assembly.
This means that if an assembly exists but lacks harmony—such as a group of merchants, a group of officials, or an army—it is not designated as the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
If there is harmony without a multitude—such as the case of two people with a single heart—it is not the Sangha Jewel.
Only when there is a multitude that is harmonious and unified does it become a cause for merit; only then is it called the Sangha Jewel.

Regarding "harmony," there are six kinds: namely, harmony of body through common practice; harmony of speech through common silence; harmony of mind through common forbearance; harmony of precepts through common cultivation; harmony of views through common understanding; and harmony of material benefits through common distribution.
In the teachings of the Confucians, the petty man and the superior man may either be harmonious or identical; now, the śrāvakas and bhikṣus are both harmonious and identical.
As for what is called the "ten directions," the Dharma has no limits or boundaries—how could it distinguish between the near and the distant?
"Assembly of monks" (saṃgha) is a redundant transliteration of both Chinese and Sanskrit; this reflects the clumsiness of the translators.
As for the fifteenth day of the seventh month, it is the conclusion of the three-month summer retreat (varṣā), and therefore the *pravāraṇā* ceremony may be performed.
The *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) occurs on three days—either the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth; here, the middle one is being cited.

The inclusion of the word "monks" (*saṃgha*) is superfluous; its removal would leave the sentence incomplete, which is likewise the fault of the translator. Why not say instead, "at the time of the communal *pravāraṇā*"?
Regarding "self-indulgence" (*pravāraṇā*): it means that one freely allows others to point out one's own transgressions.

This refers to the ninety-day intensive practice during the summer retreat; even if one does not attain the four fruits of the path, one may still achieve the four dhyānas. Such was the original intent behind the Buddha’s establishment of this teaching.
The same applies to the Sangha of the True, Semblance, and Final Dharma periods; for even in the final five hundred years, there will still be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit.

Nevertheless, as one prepares to cross the ocean of suffering, one must carefully protect the life-preserving bag (the precepts). Yet, fearing that the one standing in the midst of the fray may lose their way, it is essential to rely on the observations of bystanders regarding gain and loss.

Even though they have not severed their afflictions or realized the fruits of the path, they still hope for the extinction of their transgressions and the arising of merit; therefore, baring one shoulder in the midst of the assembly, they address the virtuous elders:
"Whether you have seen my faults, heard of my offenses, or suspect me of having committed a transgression, please feel free to bring them forth."
"Have pity on me and speak to me; I shall then repent.
If one acts thus, body and mind will become pure like lapis lazuli, and one may attain meditative concentration and liberation.
The efficacy of making offerings to this [image] can thus be known; how could it not rescue and deliver deceased ancestors and provide spiritual nourishment for those currently living?
Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master said:

"On the day monks observe the *varṣā* (the end of the rainy season retreat) and when the great assembly performs the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation for critique), many members of the Saṃgha attain the four fruits of the Path; thus, they are able to deliver their kin from calamity for seven generations."
2. Generating the Superior Resolve:
"I shall act for the sake of my parents of seven lifetimes past and those currently in distress. The phrase "I shall act for the sake of" refers to the mind capable of rescuing them.
Regarding "seven generations" below, this refers to the realm of those one rescues.
It is called "superior" because it clarifies the mind by way of its objective realm.
As for "seven generations," these refer to one's parents from whom one was born, which differs from the Confucian practice of selecting ancestors from preceding dynasties.
Those in distress and calamity include both the living and the deceased.

Among the dead, this refers to those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; among the living, it includes those afflicted by illness and pain or subjected to shackles and imprisonment—all these are termed "distress and calamity.
Although one's parents of seven generations may seem distant, they are all the vessels through whom one was born to cultivate the Way.
Having already received your nurturing and upbringing, how could I ever betray such profound kindness?
Thus, the Tripitaka Master said:
"When heaven and earth cover and support all things, they do not shrink from the toil of their labor; [so too must I]."
"Those who are hidden or manifest, and those submerged in the cycle of rebirth, ought by principle to respond with boundless gratitude.
Third, the preparation of superior offerings:

"Prepare meals of a hundred flavors and five fruits, water-jars for irrigation, oil, fragrant lamps and candles, couches, mats, and bedding. Place all the world's sweet and delicious things within these vessels and offer them to the assembly of virtuous monks of the ten directions."
"One who possesses food of a hundred flavors" is the general heading.

It is like a person who, having prepared a lavish spread of dishes on trays and mats to invite guests, simply says, "Eat rice"; thus, "rice" serves as the general term that encompasses all the hundred flavors.
"Hundred" is a large number and does not necessarily mean exactly one hundred.
Regarding the five kinds of fruits: first are pitted fruits, such as dates, apricots, peaches, plums, and so forth;
second are skinned fruits, such as melons, pears, crabapples, mulberries, and so forth.
Third are the three-husked fruits, such as walnuts and pomegranates.
Fourth are the chaff-fruits, such as sesame and linseed.
Fifth are the five-angled fruits, such as water chestnuts and beans.
The items above are all tasted by the tongue.
As for the basins and vessels used for drawing and pouring water—such as those used for bathing—as well as the beds, mats, and bedding, these are all experienced by the body.
"Perfume" refers to that which is smelled by the nose.
"Oil lamps and candles" refer to items used for illumination and the like, which are seen by the eyes;
they may also be used to anoint the body with fragrant oil, and thus belong to the category of the body, as is the custom in the Western Regions (India).
All that is sweet and delicious in the world likewise belongs to the tongue.
Thus far, among the objects of the five desires, only sound has been missing.

Regarding the phrase "all in the world," its intended meaning comprises two kinds of "exhaustion": namely, when one possesses wealth and status, one exhausts all that the world has, and whatever exists must be sought.
If one is poor and lowly, one should exhaust all that one's strength permits; once that is reached, one must seek further.
Thus, one knows that the quantity—whether small or great—is not fixed, but lies solely in the exhaustion of one’s heart.
This is analogous to how offerings are accepted for their sincerity and honored for their bright virtue.
Regarding the phrase "placed within a basin," this is a mistranslation of the scripture; how could items such as couches be placed inside a basin?
It should instead read, "placed within the *Ullambana* offering assembly."
The two phrases concerning "making offerings" clarify the actual practice.

According to the original intent of the sutra, one should simply offer usable items to the virtuous Sangha; it is not necessary to carve gold and jade, cut silks and brocades, or construct towering railings and frameworks.
Therefore, the Tripitaka Master said:

"You must provide the four requisites of excellent material offerings and the eight delicacies of exquisite flavor; extend your contemplation throughout the ten directions and offer worship with a mind made pure."
4. Praising the Exalted Field of Merit:

"On this day, all the holy assembly—some dwelling in mountain retreats in meditative concentration, some having attained the fruits of the four paths, some walking in meditation beneath trees, some freely employing the six supernormal powers to teach and transform śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and some great beings who are bodhisattvas of the ten stages manifesting as bhikṣus among the multitude—all with one mind receive the *pātra-bhara* (alms) food."
"The noble assembly, possessing the path of pure precepts, has virtues as vast as the ocean.

The first two lines provide a general introduction by praising the occasion in terms of the individuals present; the final two lines conclude by praising the individuals through their dignified deportment.
The methods for intermediate persons consist of five pairs, though the text does not present them in their proper order.

These are: first, the pair of dwelling in mountain retreats versus dwelling under trees; second, the pair of realizing the four fruits of the path versus the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); third, the pair of practice for one's own benefit versus practice for the benefit of others; fourth, the pair of precepts and meditative concentration for the learner (*śaikṣa*); and fifth, the pair of persons of great and small capacity, also known as the pair of the provisional and the real.

Furthermore, when summarized, these do not transcend the categories of person (pudgala) and dharma (dharma), namely the correspondence between the three trainings (trishikṣā) and the three vehicles (triyāna).
From the beginning up to the fourth fruit [of the śrāvaka path] constitutes meditative concentration (samādhi).
Next, from "or below" up to "teaching and transforming with mastery" constitutes wisdom (prajñā).
All are identical to the three phrases below: pure precepts.
The "Three Vehicles" refer to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the great beings of the ten stages.

They all share a single mind; this is the harmony of intention, meaning that when receiving offerings, they all equally exercise a sense of shame and remorse with a profound sense of respect, as well as a mind of compassion, gratitude, and the intent to provide relief.
Although people differ in rank—whether ordinary or sage—and in the excellence of their virtues, the mind they employ is one and no different; therefore, it is said that they are "the same.
"Receiving *pātra-bhara* food" refers to the food within the bowl.
In Sanskrit it is called *pātra*, which here means "an appropriate vessel"; the character "he" (和) is an error.
Nowadays, when it is simply called "bowl" (*bō*), it is an abbreviation.
When the title of a sutra uses the character "basin" (*pén*), it refers to the same thing as the *pātra*.
In translating, one follows local custom by titling this [text] "Pén" (Bowl). Since both *pén* and *bō* (patra) are vessels, the Tripiṭaka Master explained the title as "The Vessel for Salvation.
This single sentence of the sutra precisely clarifies that the virtuous monks (*bhadanta*) receive the offering of the *Ullambana* bowl during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
5. Attaining Supreme Benefits:

"Those who make offerings to such monks who have completed their *pravāraṇā* will, in this present life, see their parents, six types of relatives, and kinsmen escape the sufferings of the three miserable realms; they shall be liberated at that very moment, and clothing and food will appear spontaneously."
If one's parents are currently living, they shall enjoy happiness and prosperity for a hundred years.
If one's parents of seven generations have been reborn in heaven, they will attain sovereign birth by transformation and enter the radiant light of the celestial flowers.
This single recitation of the sutra contains two layers of meaning:
the first half refers to being freed from suffering through the power of compassionate vows;
the second half refers to attaining happiness through the power of loving-kindness vows. Within this happiness, there is a distinction between those who remain and those who have passed away.
The initial statement, "these monks who perform the *pravāraṇā*," refers to the five pairs of individuals previously mentioned.

Regarding "parents of the present life," this refers to the parents who gave birth to one's current body; it does not mean that those who are not yet deceased are called "present. Therefore, it is stated that they obtain benefit by "escaping the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*)."

Regarding the phrase "parents who are currently living and have not yet passed away," there is already a textual passage below it that says, "May they enjoy blessings and happiness for a hundred years"; thus, it should not be mentioned again.
The Tripitaka Master misunderstood this and provided a divergent interpretation, which is far from the intended meaning of the text.
The "six relations" refer to parents, siblings, and spouses.
"Kinsmen" refers to all one's in-laws and relatives, encompassing both those on the father’s and mother’s sides.
Those who "emerge from the three miserable realms and attain liberation" are collectively termed as having "departed from suffering."

Regarding "clothing and food being provided spontaneously": since those who have transmigrated from the three miserable realms are born among humans and devas, this belongs to the section on "extracting from suffering";
yet, as they may also obtain happiness, it also pertains to what follows.
If the parents are of lower status, it clarifies that they attain happiness regardless of their survival or demise; the textual characteristics are thus intelligible.
"Celestial flower radiance" refers to the light of the exquisite flowers in the heavens; it briefly indicates the signs of bliss.
2. The Ritual for Instructing the Assembly of Monks to Accept Offerings.

At that time, the Buddha commanded the assembly of monks from the ten directions that they must first offer prayers of blessing on behalf of the donor’s family, wishing that their parents for seven generations may practice the mind of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and only then accept the food.
When first receiving food, one should first place it before the Buddha in the stupa or temple.
Once the monks have finished their prayers of blessing, one may then receive the food oneself.
In this practice, the first half purifies the three karmas, while the second half fulfills the Three Jewels.

In the first part, the blessing (*pariṇāmanā*) is the verbal action (*vāk-karman*); in the middle, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the mental action (*manas-karman*); and in the latter part, receiving the food is the bodily action (*kāya-karman*).
Furthermore, in the latter part, the Buddha is represented by the stupa before which one stands; the Dharma is represented by the blessing; and the Saṃgha is represented by the receiving of the food.
One must receive [food] from another before eating; such is the rule of the Dharma, and even the word "receiving" (śe) belongs to the Dharma.
As for *tā*, it is a corruption in the borderlands; the correct term is *stūpa*, which means a high and prominent place.
In this context, the meaning encompasses both temples and stupas; stupas enshrine śarīra relics, while temples enshrine Buddha images.
Seventh, the filial son attains realization.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the assembly of great bodhisattvas were all filled with great joy.
Maudgalyāyana’s weeping and sobbing ceased completely.
Since his pure karma had been accomplished, he knew for certain that he would be freed from suffering.
Observing the cause and verifying the result, he saw that the sound did not deviate from its nature; therefore, he rejoiced and stopped his crying.
It is like being in a worldly prison and entrusting oneself to a person of great strength; once the wager of wealth has been placed, his heart is already filled with joy.
Eighth, the compassionate mother obtains benefit:
on that very day, Maudgalyāyana’s mother was immediately liberated from the suffering of an eon-long existence as a hungry ghost.
Maudgalyāyana heard the sutra and received its teachings; the offering of alms-basins (pindapātra) should properly have been arranged for another time.
That it is now said that he was liberated from the realm of hungry ghosts immediately following the sequence of the sutra’s exposition is a deficiency in the translation.
At the conclusion of the main body of the text, the compiler’s narrative should be recorded as follows:

"At that time, having heard this Dharma, Maudgalyāyana reached the fifteenth day of the seventh month and prepared a vessel-offering (*pén-gòng*). After making offerings to the *pravāraṇā* monks, his mother was immediately liberated from the suffering of a hungry ghost for one kalpa on that very day."
Thus, both the words and their meaning are fully revealed.
Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master said:
"When the filial son has presented his offerings on this morning, the compassionate mother shall have her calamities dispelled on this very day."
"How great is the power of the Sage, as swift as this!
As for the duration of years and kalpas during which those hungry ghosts undergo suffering, it shall be examined and recorded later.
III. The Section on Dissemination.
The section on circulation has three parts:
first, the request; second, the praise and request; third, the response to the request.
First, the request.
Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"My biological mother has been able to receive the power of the merit of the Triple Gem and the majestic spiritual power of the Saṃgha."
If all disciples of the Buddhas in future ages likewise offer the *bōronpén* (alms bowl) to rescue and deliver their present parents, as well as their ancestors up to the seventh generation—
would this not be appropriate?
When these words were spoken, it was also after the offerings had been presented; it was not the business of a single session.
It was only upon reaching the Pipphaliguhā that they were finally compiled together as a scripture.
Maudgalyāyana loved his own kin and extended that love to others, just as Ying Kaoshu admonished Lord Zhuang.
Second, the praise for the request.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, most excellent is your inquiry!
It was precisely what I intended to speak, yet you have asked it now.
The first phrase, which praises the inquiry as “excellent, most excellent,” indicates that it profoundly accords with the Sage’s mind.
The latter two phrases explain the reason.

Because he was about to speak when he encountered the words of inquiry, his capacity and the stimulus met in perfect harmony, resulting in a subtle and secret resonance; hence it is said that the question was "prompt."
The Buddha’s original intention was to explain that the way of filial piety is supreme, that the matter of uprooting suffering is weighty, and that the *Ullambana* Dharma is preeminent.
The World-Honored One beheld these excellent conditions and saw that the capacities of the assembly were ripe, such that they could be transformed through teaching.
3. Answering the Request, Part Five:
One, Teaching the Arising of Practice.
“Good son!...”

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, kings, crown princes, ministers, high officials, the three dukes, the hundred functionaries, or the myriad commoners who practice kindness and filial piety, they should all first, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month—the day of the Buddha’s joy and the day of the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā*—place food of a hundred flavors within an *urunda-bhājana* (alms bowl) for their present parents and their parents of the past seven generations, and offer it to the self-restrained monks of the ten directions.
"Though there may be distinctions between noble and base, and differences in the paths of monastics and laity, none—unless born by transformation or from moisture—lack a father and a mother.
Even the filial crow and the parrot understand how to repay kindness; how much more so should those of human lineage not rescue and deliver one another?"

The benefits and harms of filial piety have already been fully set forth in the profound discourses (*xuántán*); once one recognizes what is right and wrong, one must rely upon the correct path. Therefore, it is said that one "should first [act] for the sake of those who gave birth to one" and so forth.

According to the established regulations, one must certainly perform these acts; failure to do so constitutes a violation of the regulations. Thus, this also pertains to the formal teachings (*zhìjiào*), which is why the previous judgment also classified it as belonging to the Vinaya Piṭaka (*lǜzàng*).
However, although the Buddha is free from both sorrow and joy, his manifestation of delight on this day is in accordance with the conditions of sentient beings.

For the Buddha’s original purpose in appearing in the world was solely to exhort people to practice; he feels sorrow when seeing people commit evil and joy when seeing them cultivate goodness. Now that the ninety-day period of intensive practice by the bhikṣus has reached its conclusion, their sincerity is redoubled.
Throughout the trichiliocosm, all are likewise thus; this accords with the Buddha’s original intent—how could one not rejoice?
The merit of making offerings on this day is truly immense.
Second, the instruction to make a vow.
"I pray that my present parents may live for a hundred years free from illness and all afflictions of suffering;
and that my parents of up to seven generations may leave behind the sufferings of the hungry ghosts and be reborn among humans and devas, where their merit and joy shall be boundless."
"What is cultivated must rely on the gateway of practice, and what is attained must proceed from one's vows.
A vow is the mind’s aspiration and desire; it is the wish that both the living and the deceased may all be at peace.
For those who remain among the living, it means preserving their lifespan in the human realm and remaining forever free from illness and affliction."
For those who have passed away, their spirits are transferred to the heavens, forever severing the path of darkness.
As practice and vows support one another, there is nothing that is not beneficial.
Third, the constant performance of the teachings.

"Those disciples of the Buddha who cultivate filial piety and obedience should, in every thought-moment, constantly remember their parents, even up to their parents for seven generations. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month each year, they should always recall their birth-giving parents with filiality and compassion, and prepare an *urunda-bhājana* (alms bowl) to offer to the Buddhas and the Sangha, thereby repaying the kindness and love shown by their parents in raising them."

Those disciples of the Buddha who cultivate filial piety and obedience, conversely clarify that they are not disciples of the Buddha and are unfilial; thus, even if one is filial, one does not establish the offering of the basin.
To "constantly remember in every thought" means there is no beginning or end.
This matter is nurtured, and this mind is characterized by loving-kindness; therefore, one first initiates practice and arouses the aspiration for enlightenment to repay it.
The remainder of the text is easily understood.
The Tripiṭaka Master said:
"Parents' bonds of affection do not leave the mind for even a single thought-moment;
a filial child repaying their kindness must provide offerings without ceasing year after year.
4. Exhortation to Receive and Maintain [the Precepts].
"If all disciples of the Buddha should uphold this Dharma.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One accepts it through the power of faith and maintains it through the power of mindfulness."
"Regarding 'now to receive' (*feng*), it carries the meaning of acceptance.
'Should' (*yingdang*) exhorts these two powers.
Fifth, to joyfully accept the command."
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the fourfold assembly of disciples rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As for the "fourfold assembly," they refer to monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; alternatively, some say they include humans, devas, nāgas, and ghosts—the latter two categories are retained here to account for both possibilities.
Yet all living beings rely upon their parents for support; thus, parental kindness is equal to that of Heaven and Earth.

Although one may be a person of supreme filial piety, if they do not find the proper way, they cannot fulfill it. Now, having received this divine method, its spiritual efficacy is known with certainty: it will surely be able to eliminate the calamities of seven generations and repay the arduous labors of one’s two parents.
Knowing that my mind was inclined toward this, I joyfully accepted the command.

This concludes the *Commentary on the Ullambana Sūtra*, Part II. Master Guifeng Zongmi of the Tang Dynasty compiled essential words on filial piety to annotate this sūtra, extensively clarifying the true filiality of the Buddhist school. He enabled students to find the means to repay their parents, ensuring they do not fall into heterodox interpretations or deviant paths, but enter the Buddha’s Supreme Vehicle.

Therefore, eminent monks of successive dynasties, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, would entice both monastics and laypeople to establish the *Ullambana* assembly as a raft for delivering their ancestors; this was indeed in accordance with the commentaries on this sutra.

Qing joined with the licentiate Xu Xudong in establishing a Dharma-propagation assembly. Among the three hundred fascicles of texts they were collecting for publication, this memorial had not yet been carved into woodblocks; consequently, Li Taipu donated funds to have it engraved.

I have compared the Northern and Southern editions of the Tripitaka and found that their wording differs. I have now carved this edition based on the definitive version established by the Great Master Yunqi.

The Master has provided his own unique insights by dividing the text into topical sections; however, as the discrepancies between the Northern and Southern versions are too numerous to record here, I have appended these few words of commentary so that readers may not only recognize the differences in the wording, but might also—by following the finger—to see the moon, thereby grasping the essence of the Buddha’s great filial piety and the repayment of parental kindness.
This is the fulfillment of my aspiration.

A brief biography of the Master of the Commentary, compiled by the śramaṇa Jiqing of Xueshan in Chishui, Guizhou. Regarding this brief biography of the Master of the Commentary: according to the two texts, the *Xiaoheng chao* and the *Chuan deng lu*, Chan Master Zongmi of Mount Gui at Zhongnan Mountain was a native of Xichong County in Guozhou; his surname was He, and he was born in the first year of the Jianzhong era of the Tang dynasty.
In his childhood, he mastered the Confucian classics; upon reaching the age of twenty, he delved into the Buddhist scriptures.

In the second year of the Yuanhe era, while preparing to take the imperial examinations, he happened to visit the Dharma seat of Master Daoyuan in Suizhou. Finding a profound resonance with the Master, he sought ordination; that same year he received full precepts and was transmitted the seal of the mind.
Furthermore, he traveled extensively to seek out renowned masters, thereby broadening his knowledge and insight.

He authored commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda Śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Ullambana Sūtra*, the *Dharmadhātudarśana*, and the *Pratideśanā Sūtra*. Additionally, he compiled the sayings of Chan from various schools into the *Chan Yuan Chuan* (Exposition of the Source of Chan), along with letters, verses, and treatises in response to inquiries. Altogether, these works comprise over one hundred fascicles, all of which have been transmitted to the world.

During the Taihe era of Emperor Wenzong, he was summoned to the palace by imperial decree and granted the purple robe; the Emperor repeatedly inquired about the essentials of the Dharma, and court officials were filled with admiration.

Soon thereafter, he requested to return to the mountains. On the sixth day of the first month of the first year of the Huichang era, he passed away while seated in the pagoda courtyard of Xingfu Temple; the fourfold assembly wailed so loudly that their lamentation resounded across the wilds.
He was enshrined in his entirety at Mount Kūṅ (Kwŏngsŏng); upon cremation, several dozen śarīra relics were obtained—lustrous, large, and brilliant—which were enshrined in a stone chamber.
His secular age was sixty-two, and his monastic seniority was thirty-four.
Emperor Xuanzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dinghui and named his stupa Qianlian (Blue Lotus).
He once composed a verse which says:
"To perform deeds of meaningful purpose is the awakened mind."
To perform meaningless deeds is a state of deranged mind.
When one follows the whims of a deranged mind, one will be dragged away by karma at the moment of death;
when one awakens and does not follow such whims, one can transform karma at the moment of death.
